meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The Lion Sleeps Tonight'?
meta.ogDescription: Not The Tokens. First recorded in 1939 as "Mbube" by Solomon Linda's Original Evening Birds for Gallo in Johannesburg.

answer.label: Not a Tokens original — a 1939 Gallo 78 by Solomon Linda’s Original Evening Birds
answer.originalArtistDates: Zulu a cappella group from Johannesburg, recording from the late 1930s · led by Solomon Linda (1909–1962)
answer.sourceLine: The Tokens’ 1961 RCA Victor single is the version almost everyone means by “The Lion Sleeps Tonight,” and it is routinely treated as the song’s point of origin. It is not: the record was cut in 1939 at Gallo’s Johannesburg studio by Solomon Linda’s Original Evening Birds, under the Zulu title “Mbube,” and issued on 78 by the Gallo Record Company. Linda improvised the melody in the studio and is the composer; George David Weiss later wrote the English adaptation, with Hugo Peretti, Luigi Creatore and Albert Stanton also credited on the hit. Linda sold his rights to Gallo for ten shillings, died in 1962 with roughly forty dollars’ worth of savings, and only received formal co-composer credit after his family’s heirs settled with Abilene Music in 2006.

original.released: Issued in 1939 on a 78 rpm disc by the Gallo Record Company under the Zulu title “Mbube,” recorded at Gallo’s Johannesburg studio — reportedly in three takes with no rehearsal.
original.charted: No chart placing — South Africa had no pop chart of the kind in 1939. The record instead sold more than 100,000 copies across Africa over the following nine years, an extraordinary figure for the market and era.
original.writer: Solomon Linda (original); George David Weiss (English adaptation)
original.cover: The Tokens, RCA Victor, October 1961, released as the B-side of “Tina” with George David Weiss’s English adaptation. It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became the version the world knows.

trail: Wikipedia’s account of the song ↗ places the first recording at Gallo Recording Studios in 1939 by Solomon Linda’s Original Evening Birds, and dates The Tokens’ RCA Victor single to October 1961.

Linda’s own biography ↗ records that he was working as a packer at Gallo when he improvised the song, sold his rights for ten shillings, and died in 1962 leaving an estate his family could not stretch to a headstone.
MusicBrainz’s work entry ↗ lists Solomon Linda as both composer and lyricist of “Mbube,” in Zulu.
Wikidata ↗ describes the song as written and composed by Solomon Linda and originally recorded in 1939.

authors.name: Solomon Linda’s Original Evening Birds
authors.heading: The 1939 record
authors.metaLine: South African Zulu a cappella group, Johannesburg · recorded for Gallo Record Company
authors.bio: A sharply dressed Johannesburg vocal group — Solomon Linda singing soprano above Gilbert Madondo, Boy Sibiya and a bass trio — who worked the competitive choir circuit and recorded for Gallo, where Linda had a day job as a record packer. Their “Mbube” was captured in 1939 without rehearsal and went on to sell over 100,000 copies in Africa across the following nine years. The Zulu word gave its name to an entire vocal genre. It is the record every later version descends from.

authors.name: The Tokens
authors.heading: The 1961 hit
authors.metaLine: American vocal group from Brooklyn, New York · RCA Victor
authors.bio: The Tokens cut their version for RCA Victor in 1961, where it went out in October as the B-side of “Tina” and climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Their arrangement — the soaring wordless soprano line over doo-wop harmony — is a genuinely inspired piece of pop record-making, and it is the reason the tune is known worldwide. The only error is chronological: they were covering a song that had already travelled from Johannesburg to New York by way of The Weavers.

authors.name: Solomon Linda & George David Weiss
authors.heading: The credits
authors.metaLine: Solomon Linda (1909–1962), composer of “Mbube” · George David Weiss (American songwriter), English adaptation
authors.bio: Linda composed and improvised the melody in the Gallo studio, then signed his rights over to Eric Gallo for ten shillings, apparently without grasping what he was giving away. Weiss wrote the English adaptation that The Tokens sang, and the 1961 credit ran to Peretti, Creatore and Stanton as well. Linda died in Johannesburg in 1962 and his family could not afford a headstone; his heirs sued in 2004 and settled with Abilene Music in 2006, which finally put his name on the song as co-composer.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong origin
misattribution.intro: The Tokens’ 1961 single is so dominant that it is usually assumed to be where the song began. The record it descends from was made in South Africa more than two decades earlier.

items.why: Their RCA Victor single, issued in October 1961 as the B-side of “Tina,” topped the Billboard Hot 100 and became the definitive version worldwide. It is a cover, not the origin.
Recorded as “Mbube” at Gallo’s Johannesburg studio in 1939 and released on 78 by the Gallo Record Company. It sold over 100,000 copies in Africa in the nine years that followed.
Their December 1951 “Wimoweh” — Pete Seeger’s misheard transcription of the Zulu chorus — reached No. 6 in America and is the route by which the melody reached The Tokens.

context.heading: How a Johannesburg 78 became an American No. 1
lead: The path is unusually well documented for a song this old. “Mbube” was a hit inside South Africa on Gallo’s label, and a copy of the 78 reached New York, where Pete Seeger transcribed the Zulu chorus by ear — misheard it, in fact, which is how The Weavers’ 1951 record came to be called “Wimoweh.” That version reached No. 6 on the American charts and put the melody into the folk repertoire. The Tokens were working from that lineage, not from Linda’s record.

What let the cover eclipse the original was not the music but the paperwork. Linda had already sold his rights for ten shillings, so when the tune became one of the most lucrative in pop, the money flowed to publishers and adapters in New York rather than to the man who invented it. By the time the family reached a settlement in 2006, Linda had been dead for decades and the song had earned an estimated fifteen million dollars, of which his heirs had seen a few thousand.
detailsBody: 1939 — Solomon Linda’s Original Evening Birds record “Mbube” at Gallo’s studio in Johannesburg, reportedly in three takes with no rehearsal. It is issued on 78 by the Gallo Record Company.
Linda sells his rights in the song to Eric Gallo for ten shillings shortly after the session.
Over the following nine years the record sells more than 100,000 copies in Africa, and “mbube” becomes the name of a whole style of Zulu vocal music.
December 1951 — The Weavers release “Wimoweh,” Pete Seeger’s phonetic rendering of the Zulu chorus. It reaches No. 6 on the American charts.
October 1961 — The Tokens’ “The Lion Sleeps Tonight,” with George David Weiss’s English adaptation, is issued by RCA Victor as the B-side of “Tina” and goes to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1962 — Linda dies in Johannesburg of kidney failure. His bank balance is worth roughly forty dollars in today’s money.
2004 — Linda’s family sues over the song’s use in Disney’s The Lion King.
February 2006 — Abilene Music settles ahead of trial: back royalties from 1987, a share of future income, a trust for the heirs, and formal co-composer credit for Solomon Linda.
context.pull: The record everyone knows is a cover of a cover.
